description_ru: Рассказ о ночном поезде, случайной попутчице и торте, который нужно доставить во что бы то ни стало.
text:
The night train from Warsaw to Vienna was almost empty, and Daniel Reeves, who had spent eleven hours in meetings, was grateful for it. He found his compartment, threw his bag onto the upper bunk and was just about to close the door when a small woman in a green coat appeared in the corridor. She was carrying a large white cardboard box with both arms, as if it contained something alive. "Excuse me," she said in careful English, "I think this is my compartment too."

Her name was Halina, and she was seventy-four. She explained that she was travelling to Vienna to see her daughter, whom she had not met for nineteen years. The two women had quarrelled over something that neither of them could now remember clearly, and the silence had grown heavier with every birthday that was missed. "It is stupid," Halina said, "to lose so many years because of a few words." Daniel, who had not spoken to his own brother since the spring, found that he had nothing clever to say.

The box, she told him, contained a cake. It was a poppy-seed roll, the kind that her daughter used to ask for every Christmas. Halina had baked it herself at four o'clock that morning, and she had been guarding it ever since. At the station a porter had tried to take it away to the luggage van, and she had refused so fiercely that he had given up. "I was not going to let a stranger carry my apology," she said.

Around midnight the train stopped at the border, and two officials in thick jackets knocked on the door. They asked to see passports, and then one of them noticed the box. He wanted to know whether it contained any food. Halina answered that it contained nothing but love and sugar. The official did not smile, but the other one, who was younger, whispered something, and the box was waved through. Daniel suspected that it had been the smell of the poppy seeds that had decided the matter.

Back in the compartment, Halina turned out to be an excellent talker. In her working life she had been a translator in a publishing house, and she had learned, she said, that every language has a word for something the others cannot say. In Polish, for example, it was possible to be homesick for a person who was still alive. Daniel, who spoke only English and a little bad French, wrote the idea down on the back of his ticket, and she watched him with the satisfaction of a teacher whose pupil has finally started to listen.

After the train started moving again, neither of them could sleep. Halina took out a thermos of tea and offered him a cup. She asked what had brought him to Warsaw, and he admitted that he had come for a contract that he did not really want. He had been told by his manager that it would be good for his career. "And is that important to you?" she asked. He thought about it for a long time. The wheels went on clicking beneath them, and the dark fields slid past the window.

"When I was young," Halina said at last, "I believed that people should be punished for their mistakes. Now I think that most of us are simply tired and frightened. It is very easy to wait for the other person to speak first. It is much harder to be the one who knocks on the door." She looked at the box on her knees. "Of course, it may be that she will not even open it."

At six o'clock in the morning the train pulled into Vienna under a pale, cold sky. Daniel carried her suitcase onto the platform, because she would not let anybody touch the cake. A tall woman with grey in her hair was standing near the clock, her hands deep in her pockets. She did not move when she saw them. Halina stopped too. For a moment the two of them simply looked at each other, and Daniel felt that he ought not to be watching.

Then the daughter took one step forward, and another, and then she was running. Halina nearly dropped the box. Somebody laughed, and somebody else began to clap, and Daniel realised that the clapping was coming from the two sleepy officials who had changed trains with them. He picked up the suitcase and walked quietly away, giving them the privacy they deserved.

On the way out of the station he took out his phone and looked at his brother's number for a while. It was seven o'clock, far too early to call anybody. He called anyway. The phone rang four times, and Daniel could hear his own heart in his ears. Then a sleepy voice said, "Do you know what time it is?" and Daniel, smiling for the first time in months, answered that he did, and that he was sorry, and that he was bringing a cake.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Кончик языка между зубами и включите голос; не произносите «з» или «д».
Язык не касается нёба и не вибрирует; губы слегка округлены, без русского «р».
Не оглушайте конечный звонкий звук: в «bag» и «old» голос сохраняется до конца слова.
После начального «p, t, k» добавляйте лёгкий выдох, как будто дуете на свечу.

questions.question: Where was Halina travelling and why?
questions.answer: To Vienna, to see her daughter after nineteen years.

questions.question: What did the box contain?
questions.answer: A poppy-seed cake that she had baked herself.

questions.question: Why was Daniel in Warsaw?
questions.answer: He had gone for a contract that he did not really want.

questions.question: What did Daniel do at the end of the story?
questions.answer: He phoned his brother to apologise.
